items.question: How do you see the difference between New York’s DUMBO neighborhood and Times Square?
items.object: DUMBO and Times Square in New York
items.answer: I think DUMBO is, of course, very artistic, right? It appears in many movies. There was a Korean movie we saw before called Past Lives; you may have seen the carousel they filmed, and the DUMBO bridge over there, right? Oh, only tourists go to Times Square.

items.answer: There are various reasons, I think. Of course, I really aspired to this city—to many of its elements, its people—and NYU as well. items.question: How do you see yourself as a podcast guest, given how much you enjoy listening to podcasts?
items.object: Participating in podcasts as a guest versus listening to them
items.answer: I don’t know. I think I’m better suited to being a listener. I really like podcasts. I listen to a lot of podcasts; on Spotify and YouTube, every day on my commute, before bed, and whenever I have free time, I listen to some podcasts. I think it’s also very enjoyable when I pull my students together to chat in everyday life. But this podcast thing—I don’t know. Maybe nobody invited me.

items.question: How did the arrival of the internet change your experience of learning and expressing yourself as a child?
items.object: The arrival of the internet during Saining Xie’s childhood
items.answer: I do think our generation’s experience of growing up was quite different. Of course, I don’t know—children today may feel the same way in this AI era. But when I was about nine, I got my first computer. At first I didn’t use it for anything serious; I bought games box by box and played them. Later, the internet came along, and for the first time I felt this explosion of information. That was when I first learned what content was, and suddenly felt I had more ways to express myself, because reading is still a one-way learning process. It is broadening too, but online there were BBS forums where you could publish your opinions. I remember Sina blogs—maybe they don’t even exist anymore—but I wrote a great many blog posts.

items.question: How do you see your own academic trajectory compared with the conventional path through elite schools and universities?
items.object: His academic trajectory and the conventional elite academic path
items.answer: I now have many, many friends who were all on an A-class path from start to finish. The best high schools, the best undergraduate programs, competitions, the best PhDs, and then teaching at, say, Stanford afterward—a very clear main track, right? I admire them greatly. I was absolutely not like that. At most, I had a B-class trajectory. And many of my decisions were rather metaphysical, because I don’t think I deliberately pursued things within some meritocratic setting or framework. A lot of it was actually quite random. Maybe there was no way around it; maybe my IQ wasn’t high enough.

items.question: How do you look back on your decision to accept early admission to Shanghai Jiao Tong University instead of taking the gaokao?
items.object: His decision to accept early admission to Shanghai Jiao Tong University
items.answer: Being recommended for admission, for example, was also quite accidental. I happened to have two awards in psychology and mathematics competitions, and SJTU happened to have a plan that allowed students to enter early—basically to scoop up some students and keep them from taking the gaokao. I had actually been trained very much within the gaokao framework; originally, I should have taken the gaokao. So I struggled over it for quite a long time. Schoolteachers would say, “No, this won’t do. How can you desert at the last minute? Your grades are good too, right? Of course you should make a push for Tsinghua or Peking University.” But internally I thought, SJTU is quite good. I had been to Shanghai, and I felt I was temperamentally aligned with the city and the university. I wanted to study computer science, and I thought SJTU’s computer science was pretty good at the time. I had also heard of a program like ACM. Although the selection process then required you to enter early, attend something like a summer camp, take tests, and only then enter the class. But many interesting things happened in that process. If I had to choose again, I would have absolutely no regrets. The summer when I entered early was the highlight of my life.

items.question: How do you understand your own academic trajectory when you compare yourself with the highest-achieving students?
items.object: Academic self-perception and the experience of attending Shanghai Jiao Tong University (SJTU)
items.answer: It depends on whom I compare myself with, right? Compared with the very top competition contestants—the people I just described with that very smooth path, the Yao Class prodigies, the top four PhDs and professors at the top four schools—I really was far, far behind. But on the other hand, I’m very grateful for that entire experience, because as we continue the story, I think it’s quite interesting. When I went to SJTU, it wasn’t necessarily a school that was particularly leading in computer science or AI. But now the A3 class has become something—of course, this has nothing to do with me—but my juniors, my seniors, whether they are doing startups or academic work, are shining in various places. We have a strong alumni network; everyone is connected and gets things done. I think it has been an upward trajectory.

items.question: Why do you see your A3 class admissions interview as a predestined connection to NYU’s Courant Institute?
items.object: The connection between the A3 class admissions interview and NYU’s Courant Institute
items.answer: The A3 class had interviews. Professor Shen Renshao, an older professor at the time, interviewed us. The interview did not ask technical questions; he asked what books you liked to read. I think there was some predestined connection in this, because I was very anxious at the time and almost couldn’t answer. I told him that a book I really liked, and had just finished reading, was What Is Mathematics? Professor Shen then asked, “So who wrote it?”—to test me. I was a little stunned. As a high-school student, I couldn’t remember foreign names very well. I thought, and finally answered: Richard Courant. Professor Shen said, “Yes, you must remember this name, because he was one of the greatest mathematicians of the twentieth century.” Why do I feel that this was fate, or a coincidence? Because the department and institute I’m in at NYU now is the Courant Institute of Mathematical Sciences—the department that Richard Courant built, the one for which he put the first shovel in the ground. So I think that’s quite interesting.

items.question: Why do you consider Xiaodi Hou’s publication at CVPR as an undergraduate at a mainland Chinese university so remarkable for its time?
items.object: Xiaodi Hou’s undergraduate CVPR publication
items.answer: CVPR now accepts perhaps thousands and thousands of papers each year, from tens of thousands of submissions. So now when we recruit undergraduates, everyone having three, four, or five CVPR papers is no longer remarkable. But at that time, at a university in mainland China, publishing work at such a top conference was extremely, extremely difficult. Very rare. And for an undergraduate to publish work like that was unheard of, so everyone truly admired him enormously.

items.question: What do you find interesting about the SJTU Student Survival Guide?
items.object: SJTU Student Survival Guide
items.answer: I reread it the other day, and some passages were very, very interesting. What was it about? It was about why people study, what is wrong with China’s educational system and university model, and where you should spend your time to achieve the life you want. Or it also guided people on how to do research and what research is for. The point of research is not padding output with papers; it is truly exploring the infinite unknown—things like that. Of course, it also taught people how to skip class and how to finish assignments, how to complete some assignments more quickly. It was a little handbook.

items.question: Why did vision attract you so strongly as a subject for AI research?
items.object: Vision as a way of experiencing the world
items.answer: Because vision is how I experience the world. As a child, perhaps because I was bored, I would think: people have so many senses; if I absolutely had to remove one, which would I remove? Maybe I could not hear, maybe I could not speak, maybe I would have no touch or smell. I would live miserably, but perhaps it would still be acceptable. But if I had no vision, I could not watch cartoons, movies, or play games. It seems I would lose a person’s independence. I think those initial thoughts aligned quite well with things I later read in books. Think about it: visual signals occupy—depending on how you put it—the major visual areas may account for 30 percent of the brain, while when you see an image, activated areas may account for 70 percent of the whole brain. So all of us are visual animals. That’s how I see it. I’m a visual animal too, and I really like looking at things.

items.question: How do you understand the evolutionary importance of vision beyond humans?
items.object: Vision as an evolutionary arms race and a proposed driver of the Cambrian explosion
items.answer: I think this is not something unique to humans; all animals are like this. Though it wasn’t entirely like this: 530 million years ago, living things on Earth did not have eyes. Everyone lived in the deep sea, in perpetual darkness; light could not reach them. Then one day, some organisms developed vision. It was still weak—they could only see a faint signal. But then they became powerful: they could see where what they wanted to prey on was, swim quickly over, and eat it. They could also avoid predators. If someone came to catch me, I would immediately flee. Once vision arose, other organisms had to evolve stronger vision in the course of evolution, because if you did not have stronger vision, you would be eaten. So an arms race unfolded. This was the so-called Cambrian explosion. The so-called Cambrian era. Before the Cambrian, there may have been only a handful of species on Earth; after it, suddenly, as if in an explosion, there were hundreds of thousands more species. One leading theory is that the source of this explosion was precisely this arms race over vision.

items.question: How do you make sense of your own path into computer vision research?
items.object: Chance, destiny, and individuality in a researcher's path
items.answer: Actually, nothing much happened. I think a lot of it came from chance. If I had perhaps not read that book, I might not have gone down this path. But sometimes I think that is also inevitable. I still quite believe that everyone has their own destiny. Or, I sometimes tell students: don’t think that if you do not do something, someone else will do it. Think instead that if you do not do it, it will never happen in this world. What does that mean? Say you are working on a research topic. You do it; how do you reach that endpoint step by step? It depends entirely on your previous personal life experience and background of growth: perhaps a book you read, perhaps a conversation you had with someone, perhaps genetically—your genes, in other words—you are simply different from others. I think every individual is very distinct in this world.

items.question: Why do you hold Professor Tu and his generation of computer vision researchers in such high regard?
items.object: Professor Tu’s mentorship and the pioneering generation of computer vision researchers
items.answer: I think it was also that he saved me. Not only did he pull me up at the beginning; later, in research during my PhD, he really helped me. You can regard my internship in Singapore and so on as doing some research, but in fact it was still small-scale tinkering. It feels different to have someone beside you teaching you how to work. Professor Tu was the kind of professor who sat beside your monitor and went through code with you line by line. And he often spoke of this with pride, and I think he fully deserved to be proud. Several works he published that had an important influence on later computer vision were completed independently by him as sole author. Back then there was none of what we have now: PyTorch, so many open-source communities and libraries to call on, GPUs. In his time there was nothing; he had to write from the bottom up. For example, for an image-segmentation task, he wrote everything from scratch—about fifty thousand lines of code—and he showed me the code. It included the most foundational things, including distributed training and a whole series of things, all written in C++. On the one hand, I feel very, very fortunate not to have had to go through that. On the other hand, I think scientists and professors of their generation in the United States are truly admirable. Without them, there would be no us today. They blazed a trail. As I said, publishing a CVPR paper had originally been extremely difficult, and there was a certain fixed circle. It took Professor Tu, his advisor Professor Song-Chun Zhu, and later Professor Fei-Fei and others to blaze that trail, so that we would have a path to follow.

items.question: How do you understand the benefit of having multiple exits in Deeply Supervised Nets?
items.object: Deeply Supervised Nets
items.answer: The way I would explain it is: you have an input and get an output. Deeply Supervised Nets says that you can instead have multiple branches: a neural network can have multiple exits, and you can apply a supervisory signal at each exit. One direct benefit is that you do not have to do backpropagation only from the farthest signal all the way back to the early layers. You do not have to backpropagate from the far end all the way to the very beginning. You can backpropagate from an intermediate node, which resolves part of the vanishing-gradient problem.

items.question: How did your work on Holistic Edge Detection change your understanding of deep learning?

items.answer: It opened up many ideas for me, because I realized that every layer of a neural network has implicit structure and information. Again, a neural network does not only have inputs and outputs; there is much information in the middle, and it represents a hierarchical structure of the world. For edge detection, that means the edges output by lower layers are coarser edges. As you go upward, the edges become more detailed. Finally, you can fuse all these edges and obtain an output that is closest to the human understanding of edges. I think this gave me a new understanding of deep learning.

items.answer: The reason is that it is like planting a tree. Your representations are the roots. Once the tree grows, it needs different branches. Each branch is a different downstream application. I have done image recognition, image segmentation, edge detection, video recognition, action recognition, and even, later on, some embodied-RL-related tasks. items.question: How has your understanding of neural network architecture's role in representation learning changed?
items.object: The roles of neural network architecture, data, and objectives in representation learning
items.answer: So I think the starting point of all this, if we trace it back, of course involves deep learning and the design of deep neural network architectures. I think this part is certainly related to representation learning. And this is also a direction that everyone has been working hard on in the past—not just me, right? Everyone has been doing this: how to design a better architecture so that we can learn better representations, so that we can solve problems better. Right? And later on, actually, I think things begin to change. You realize that architecture itself may not be the most important thing. It is certainly important, but it may not be the most important thing, or rather, it cannot be the whole story. At least several different things are intertwined, right? Architecture is one thing—your architecture is one part—and then your data are also very important. And then your objective, your goal, is also important, right? I think the architecture determines what you train with. We can imagine this as having a huge engine, and the hardware of that engine may be the architecture of a neural network. But having only the architecture of such an engine is useless; without fuel, you cannot start it, right? So there are considerations at the data level and at the objective level—the loss-function level. And so my subsequent research has also followed this main thread of representation learning, moving forward around architecture, data, and objectives.

items.question: How do you assess the strengths and limitations of learning visual representations through ImageNet-style supervised classification?
items.object: The strengths and limitations of ImageNet-style supervised representation learning
items.answer: With ImageNet, I have one thousand classes and can directly train a supervised classifier, obtaining a representation that way. In the previous era, that was what everyone did. Through labels for one thousand classes. By the way, two hundred of those one thousand classes are different breeds of dogs. Even so, that is why ImageNet is so powerful, right? Even with that distribution, it still enabled our neural networks to learn very good representations. I think that is extremely impressive. But people could also see its limitation: once everything is only supervised learning, there are many things you cannot characterize. Because of what it learns. For example, we are sitting here now and see these chairs, right? We have vast numbers of images of different chairs. Some chairs may be ordinary chairs in a studio like this; some may be chairs at home; some may be designer chairs; or an avocado chair, a chair that looks like an avocado. For supervised learning, you need to map all of this to one label. That label is called “chair.” So the mapping the network has to learn is actually extremely difficult.

items.question: Why do you see self-supervised learning as a way for computer vision systems to acquire common sense?
items.object: Self-supervised learning in computer vision
items.answer:
A common misunderstanding in the past was: “We want to do unsupervised learning because labeling data is too hard and too expensive. We need to hire people to label it; it costs money and time; we do not want to do that.” But that is only a very, very small issue. The big issue, in the eyes of computer-vision researchers, was that people knew very early on that this path alone could not give an AI system this kind of common sense.

So in 2015 and 2016, people were extremely creative. That period was quite a creative era: people designed all kinds of miscellaneous tasks. For example, you take an image and rotate it by 90 degrees, 180 degrees, or 270 degrees. You do not give those images a label, but because you designed how the images are rotated, the images and their rotation angles can form a valid pretext task. You can predict how many degrees an image was rotated; that becomes a proxy task. Similar proxy tasks include taking an image, turning it grayscale, removing all its color, and then using a neural network to reconstruct the original colors—essentially predicting from a grayscale image what color each object should be. And there are countless similar examples.

One final example is the so-called context encoder: I cut out a patch in the middle of an image and make it white. The task is to train a neural network to fill in that hole. The basis for all these pretext tasks is that we believe humans can do these things. Humans can tell whether an image was rotated by 90 or 180 degrees, what color a butterfly or a house in an image should have, or can predict missing information in the middle, because they have some understanding of the physical world; they have common sense. So they can infer how corrupted signals—signals that have been lost—should be reconstructed.

items.question: Why do you distrust research ideas that come from simply sitting and thinking?

items.answer: This paradigm is also something Kaiming taught me. He said you cannot just sit there and think up all these ideas. If you think up an idea while sitting there, it is definitely not a good idea. There are only a few possibilities. First, you are smarter than everyone else in the world, so you come up with a particularly brilliant idea that no one else could think of. But I think the probability of that is extremely small. items.question: How do you think researchers should approach the exploratory phase of a project to find a direction worth pursuing?
items.object: The exploratory phase of research and finding a direction
items.answer:
You cannot sit there thinking about problems. What you need to do is continually hack on things. You really have to play with things like a hacker—treat research like a game, like a toy to play with. For example, you can work through equations, read more papers, and find connections. Of course, perhaps more importantly, you need to get your hands dirty and write code. But what matters is that the code you write is not initially for your triggering idea or direction; it is part of an exploratory process. You might simply reproduce a baseline—take something from someone else's paper and reproduce it. Or you might make some extensions on top of that baseline. The most important thing is to find a signal.

The whole decision-making process is rather unordered exploration; it is what we call stochastic gradient descent, which is a foundation of all machine learning. But it also applies to research itself and to our lives: in pursuing an ultimate goal, we are all carrying out a process of stochastic gradient descent. I think research is the same. The most important thing in research is not getting from point A to point B—for example, A being an idea and B being a paper—but what signal you can find in the process, where your gradient is. So Kaiming's formulation is that the gradient itself is the real source of your idea.

When you go through continual exploration, you try many things; some may fail, some may succeed. By the way, it does not have to be a successful experiment that gives you a gradient. Sometimes a wrong experiment gives you a larger gradient, right? The most frightening thing is simply not knowing which way to go. So a good result or a bad result—both are good results for research. A surprise, a surprising observation, is always the happiest thing for a researcher.

items.question: How do you think a research idea becomes truly your own?
items.object: Developing a research idea that truly belongs to you
items.answer: With that word, “belongs,” you need to see that this thing really is your own. On the one hand, heaven gives you inspiration; on the other, it is based on a great deal of evidence and practice—that produces it, right? There is no free lunch in this. Again, maybe you really are a genius, or extremely lucky, and God holds your hand and writes down this equation. That can happen. But most of the time, most progress—even most work that has a major impact on the field—happens step by step. You can always trace it back and find its starting point. So I also tell students: what is the worst kind of research? It is when you define a problem at the beginning, say “this is my idea,” and finally publish a paper whose idea is exactly the same as the one you had at the beginning. You encountered no obstacles and no difficulties.

items.question: How do you understand the relationship between research quality and career impact through Bill Freeman's illustration?
items.object: Bill Freeman's illustration of research quality and career impact
items.answer: I think the nonlinearity of research is temporal, but in terms of results it is nonlinear too. MIT professor Bill Freeman has a very classic plot—an illustration—that he often talks about in his talks. It has a horizontal axis and a vertical axis. The horizontal axis runs from a very poor piece of work, to a fairly good piece of work, to a very good piece of work, to an extremely great piece of work. The vertical axis is the impact of that paper on your entire career. It is not a linear curve. It is not that a poor work has little career impact, then better work gives increasingly better returns in a gradual linear process. Basically, a very poor piece of work will not really hurt you either. Nobody cares. Nobody notices. Fairly good work also goes unnoticed, and brings you very little. But sometimes you produce a very good piece of work, an exceptionally great piece of work. Work that everybody knows.

items.question: Why do you think large language models will eventually fade away?

items.question: How do you understand the value of your previous research in the development of your thinking?
items.object: The value and interconnected development of his research
items.answer: Saying it this way makes it seem as though there is nothing worth discussing in these works, but I think they still have some meaning. As I just said about nonlinear research, within one paper we do some things first, then gradually build up reserves, and in the final month find a new direction and deliver the final result. When I look at all my previous work, I have that same feeling. I am still in the initial, confused exploration phase, but who knows? Maybe this year, maybe next year, maybe suddenly, you know, I have an awakening and can produce more meaningful work. But I think this year's foundation is, as I said, that it needs to connect into a thread—or rather, it is not a thread; it is a graph, with different nodes. Each node is a paper, and the nodes are interconnected. Every subsequent paper you publish will be influenced by all the earlier papers.

items.question: How did your experience with MoCo V3 and masked autoencoders shape your view of scaling self-supervised learning?
items.object: The promise and limitations of scaling self-supervised learning through MoCo V3 and MAE
items.answer:
In V3 we used a Transformer and scaled up. The representations were already much better than what ImageNet could produce across all kinds of tasks. That was a major surprise to us. At that point in time, I felt, wow, everything was flourishing again; our problems could basically be answered. We had found a way for self-supervised learning to work. Next, we only needed to scale up what we were doing, and the future would be incomparably bright. But unfortunately, that did not happen either.

Along the contrast-learning path, we kept going and found it could not scale up. We wanted to change directions, so we returned to a simpler approach: a kind of denoising autoencoder, namely a masked autoencoder. This method was even simpler. In short, it learns representations by corrupting images in some way and then reconstructing noisy, corrupted, or masked images. This is fundamentally different from contrast learning, but the results were also good. It has very different characteristics: for example, it does not explicitly model invariance, so its linear-probing results are somewhat worse; but on untuned fine-tuning—these are two different ways to test representations—the results can be much better. In short, they have different properties, and their learned representations look different too. These things later had far-reaching implications.

At that time we thought, wow, MAE is incredible. Okay, MAE should at least win a Best Paper award, right? Later it did not. Scaling MAE should solve all problems, right? Later we found it did not scale up either. It was somewhat a series of dramatic ups and downs. On the one hand we got good results; on the other, these papers were just papers. We never truly delivered something practical—something like GPT that could lead to an entirely different, scalable future paradigm. So by then, that chapter had somewhat come to an end.

items.question: What do you value about Kaiming's way of leading research?
items.object: Kaiming's research leadership and management
items.answer:
Both MoCo and MAE were projects led by Kaiming. When people say a project is “led” by someone, I think Kaiming really demonstrated leadership: he took on eighty or ninety percent of the responsibilities of both first author and last author—the corresponding author. He had to write the baseline himself, run many experiments himself, finish writing the paper, develop the story, and present it. Essentially, Kaiming did all of this single-handedly. We of course participated and contributed, but I am saying that this was a direction led by Kaiming. We accelerated its progress and may have improved the result significantly, but that does not change its essence.

Even now, for example, he told me two days ago that he really enjoys IC work—individual-contributor work. He does not enjoy managing a large team or merely being a manager who guides directions. He does not like that. He has many people; many undergraduate students come to visit him. He has now done a great deal of very good work, so I do not actually believe him. I tell him that he is actually also a very good manager. At least, although you have not truly managed me, as long as I am around you, I can feel that I work more efficiently; I feel I have become smarter. If I wanted a manager, I would hope for one like that—someone who can empower the people around them to become better. That is Kaiming, I think.

items.question: How do you assess the significance of your PointContrast work extending self-supervised learning to 3D?
items.object: PointContrast and the broader impact of self-supervised representation learning
items.answer: I could say that I extended self-supervised learning to 3D for the first time and did some work on point clouds, called PointContrast. That work was more about showing that representation learning is not merely an image-domain problem; it is a very general method, or methodology. It holds not only for images, but in 3D spaces as well. Later, many people tried it in all kinds of medical imaging, robotics tasks, and other domains, and it held up. So I do not regard it as a failure, because it did influence many different areas beyond computer vision itself. But on the other hand, it still did not achieve the kind of influence LLMs have. So after all that, what next? Right—it seemed to return to the exploration period again.

items.question: How has Kaiming’s approach to building strong baselines shaped your understanding of what enables breakthroughs in AI research?
items.object: Kaiming’s approach to building strong research baselines and infrastructure
items.answer:
At first the TPUs were for people doing language models. People tried playing with them and then found, oh dear, they were too difficult to use—really unusable. Kaiming said, “I’ll do it.” So he truly, again, single-handedly built an entire infrastructure on TPUs from beginning to end, which enabled us to do the subsequent series of work. Including MoCo, MAE, and the later DiT—all happened on TPUs. So this was also very important guidance for me. How should I summarize it? “To do a good job, one must first sharpen one’s tools.” And one thing Kaiming taught me is that the upper limit of your research depends on the quality of your baseline. If your baseline is poor, it is easy to deceive yourself; you will not be able to produce much. If you have not put enough effort into building the system well at the baseline level—taking the engineering to the limit—you do not have a platform on which to conduct real exploration. You may discover an interesting, valuable signal, but it may be completely wrong because your baseline itself is not good enough.

This is quite counterintuitive, because people always say, “If my baseline is a bit worse, I can show a larger performance gain and perhaps publish more easily.” But Kaiming does not think that way. He thinks: how can we make the baseline as high as it can possibly be? Then, anything new we do on that basis is groundbreaking. That is a genuine breakthrough, right? Any improvement you make on top of a weak baseline may be just a watered-down paper. I found that inspiring.

When they did detection—this was work I did not participate in; I was still a PhD student—all the Fast R-CNN, Mask R-CNN, Focal Loss, and related work came from extensive work by Ross, Kaiming, Wu Yuxin—whom everyone calls Kimi—and others, building the infrastructure and codebase so their baselines for these methods already far surpassed all those miscellaneous CVPR papers. You know, our baseline is already stronger than yours. If I take one more step forward, of course I will go farther than you. Right?

So I have always had this methodology. I value this kind of—I do not really want to call it engineering, because it is not merely a codebase in the sense of building one at a product company. It is more a scaffold for research breakthroughs. If your scaffold is unstable, you cannot make anything. So this also affects how we do research now. Anyway, Kaiming was truly exceptionally good at building this scaffold.

items.question: How do you think designing an Excel spreadsheet for tracking experiments shapes the research process?
items.object: Using Excel spreadsheets to design and track research experiments
items.answer: There are many better tools. But at the time, we would carefully build a template, and that template was Excel. So sometimes we were a bit like clerical workers: during research every day, it wasn't screens full of code, writing something fancy; rather, we were staring at this spreadsheet, this Excel table. Then looking at what each row actually represents. For the research part, it is about how you design this table—how you make sure every experiment gives you, as I just said, a gradient, right? There can always be two extremes. One is that you run too few experiments, so the signal is unclear—you just don't know. The other extreme is: I completely don't care what experiments I'm running; I just run them blindly, right? I have so many resources, so I maximize them, run all the jobs, dump all the results straight into the table, and feel satisfied, thinking the research is done. Both are relatively bad research patterns for students. But by watching how Kaiming built a spreadsheet like this, I learned a great deal. Because you have to make decisions: what metrics should I actually focus on? What exactly should I record—which columns?

items.question: How do you think about choosing which experimental results belong in a research spreadsheet?
items.object: Selecting experimental results for a research spreadsheet
items.answer: I have to think about what rows I should have. Which experimental results should go into the table, and which should perhaps not go in, or should be hidden? Because a row you put in has to relate to the other rows in the table. This kind of controlled comparison is the research process; again, it gives you a gradient signal. Right? And this can sometimes be extremely, extremely subtle, because it is not the case that the better your results are, the more certainly you are on the right path.

items.question: How do you judge the value of a controlled experiment when its performance gets worse?
items.object: Informative controlled experiments in research
items.answer: It is still about seeing which control gives you the greatest amount of information—maximize information. For a simple example, suppose you run an experiment and its performance drops by 10 points, right? If you are pessimistic, you say, "Ah, this experiment failed completely; forget it." But if you are someone with this kind of mindset, you think: "Oh, it can drop 10 points in this direction. If I design my algorithm in the opposite direction, could I gain a lot of points?" Because what you fear most is its performance staying where it is. Neither good nor bad, right?

items.question: How do you think about learning from the signals you get from research experiments?

items.answer: The opposite direction of a negative signal is a positive signal, and the forward direction of a positive result is also a good signal. So I find this very, very interesting. Another thing Kaiming often told us was: learn to make predictions. When I run an experiment, I should predict what its result should be.

items.question: Why do you think it is useful to predict an experiment’s result before running it?
items.object: Predicting experimental results to test one's reasoning
items.answer: Because I need to guess whether my thinking is right. If I guessed right, it means my preceding chain of thought can continue to extend and be pushed forward. If I guessed wrong, again, that is also a surprise. Right? It gives me a signal. Then I ask: why was I wrong? Right? Where did I think wrongly? I can try to explain the reasons behind it, or reassess my own line of thought.

items.question: What do you think lies at the heart of research taste?
items.object: Research taste
items.answer: I think it includes all the things I have discussed above. The concrete ways of doing things are included in it, but it also involves some higher-level philosophical considerations. Kaiming gave me the Diamond Sutra because it says all things are like dreams, illusions, bubbles, shadows, right? One passage says: "All conditioned phenomena are illusory; if one sees all appearances as non-appearances, then one sees the Tathagata." To digress a little, this is quite similar to certain views in Western philosophy, right? For example, Kant on the thing-in-itself, and Schopenhauer on the world as will and representation. I do not understand philosophy and do not want to pontificate, but in my crude understanding, what they are trying to discuss is that what you see is not the essence of the thing. What you see—the world—is not its substance either. So when you read a paper, the important thing is to break through the illusion the paper gives you and ask what substantive thing is actually implicit behind it. I think the source of research taste lies in whether people can truly set aside all these empty appearances and keep moving toward truth, keep seeking.

items.question: What do you admire about Kaiming's approach to writing research papers?
items.object: Kaiming's approach to writing research papers
items.answer: Kaiming is also the strongest writer, and he strongly encouraged us to start writing early. Unfortunately, even now, at my age, I still do not do that well. All of Kaiming's papers were finished one month before the deadline—at least that was how it was at FAIR. When everyone else was still pulling all-nighters for the deadline and getting this huge sense of satisfaction from it, Kaiming was like an idle cloud and wild crane: he had finished everything a month earlier, then polished it over and over while watching you rush to the deadline. In a very chill way, he made it as perfect as possible.

items.question: How has Kaiming's approach to polishing papers influenced your own standards for their presentation?

items.answer: One month is a long time. Of course he would keep writing afterward. In the month before the deadline, he would polish every table—every word, every punctuation mark. This also affected me. Now I have this OCD—how should I put it, compulsiveness—from the Kaiming era: no line in your paper should have less than 60 percent text. What does that mean? If most of a line is blank, it looks bad; you need to fill that line, or make it about 60 or 70 percent full.

items.question: Why do you have your students check for single words left alone on a line when finishing a paper?

items.answer: So now, at the end of every paper, I have all the students look carefully. If you have a trailing word—if you do not pay attention, you can end up with one word alone on a line somewhere. It is very ugly.

items.question: How do you think about an academic paper as a medium for communicating knowledge?
items.object: Academic papers as a medium for communicating knowledge
items.answer: Kaiming's thinking was that the paper is not for you to look at; it is for other people. So what matters is how it feels to others. A paper is only a medium: how do I use this carrier of knowledge to let people smoothly get the core that I want to express?

items.question: Why do you see writing a research paper as similar to making a movie?
items.object: Storytelling and decision-making in research papers
items.answer: The real story is not a character's background, but the choices the character makes at a particular time. That brings conflict, changes the world, and drives the plot forward. items.question: How do you assess the contribution of your ConvNeXt paper, “A ConvNet for the 2020s”?
items.object: ConvNeXt and its paper, “A ConvNet for the 2020s”
items.answer: The paper itself is very simple: people thought self-attention was the most important thing in ViT, Vision Transformer, but we questioned whether that was really true. Through that questioning, we set up the experiments and ultimately found that it was not that simple. Self-attention may be the least important part; the overall global architectural design, and macro and micro design, are more crucial to performance. Liu Zhuang ran a huge number of experiments, and together with other colleagues we clarified it. We had a figure, a plot, in the paper: how, step by step, we move from a convolutional neural network to a hierarchical Transformer architecture; which experiments matter at each step and which do not—a series of ablation studies. The paper was quite good, perhaps worthy of its title: afterward, essentially nobody designed convolutional neural network architectures anymore. This figure has become a classic illustration and its traces can be found in all kinds of papers. I spent a long time making that figure by hand.

items.question: Why did you feel it was no longer a good time to remain at FAIR as OpenAI emerged as a research leader?
items.object: FAIR’s organizational model and the decision to leave
items.answer: ChatGPT had just come out. OpenAI—and DeepMind was doing very well too. OpenAI had become an emerging research leader, doing many things that people at FAIR did not dare imagine, or could not do even if they did imagine them. People started wondering what was wrong with the organizational model and whether major reform was needed; there had already been many reworks. This was also a trigger for why I felt it was no longer a good time to remain at FAIR.

items.question: How did your exploration of diffusion-model representations lead you to recognize DiT as a direction worth pursuing?
items.object: The development of DiT and the research taste behind its architecture
items.answer: At that time, when I was working on DiT, diffusion was just getting started. Nobody at FAIR was doing research related to diffusion models. But I thought it seemed interesting and worth trying. Our starting point was not to do diffusion models, nor DiT. Our first two months of exploration were entirely focused on representation learning: we wanted to see how the representations learned by a diffusion model differed from those learned through normal supervised learning or self-supervised learning. There has since been much work in this direction, but after doing it for a while, we felt it was just okay. A generative model can learn a decent representation, but it is far, far, far worse than one learned through self-supervised learning. It cannot compete at all, so we gave it up. But in the final month, we found—by the way, the premise was that for DiT we needed to compare representations at that level with ViT-based representation systems. That is why we did not use a U-Net, but used ViT for the diffusion model—that was the starting point. Later we found there was not much value from the representation perspective, but our new architecture was indeed more efficient and scalable. It was more stable than a U-Net. From a code perspective, I care a great deal about this. We call it minimal description length: code matters and can reveal something. If your code is short yet accomplishes the same goal, your method will typically be better than a huge system with thousands of lines of code, even if it can do the same thing. The former—more elegant, simpler—solution is certainly better. I think that too is research taste in some sense. So we found: it was simple, it worked, it was scalable, and it was efficient. That seemed like the direction we should pursue, so we did it one month ahead of time. At the time we also had to compete for many resources. People said, "What are you doing this for? We need to concentrate resources and do more meaningful, bigger projects."

items.question: Why did you believe the DiT project was worth pursuing despite internal opposition?
items.object: DiT as a direction for diffusion architectures
items.answer: It had to be discussed in those alignment meetings. But at least diffusion models would not be an important part of the critical path. So there was much opposition. items.question: What was your initial reaction to Aravind’s early Perplexity demo and his ambition to revolutionize Google?
items.object: Aravind’s early Perplexity demo
items.answer: He showed me a laptop and a browser, and said, "Hey, we are going to revolutionize Google." I said, "Wow, this is amazing," but inwardly I thought, what is this? Is this not just GPT wrapped in a shell? Why are you doing this?

items.question: How do you judge your career decisions when you consider opportunities you may have missed?
items.object: His career decisions and potentially missed opportunities
items.answer: Some may have only just been missed, or I may not yet know whether I missed them—or not. But there was not really anything missed. At this point, I do not regret any decision. Every decision was relatively faithful to my heart and to doing what I wanted to do. Some decisions may have been foolish, and by some measures may have been wrong. But now, first, I feel content; second, this is my own path. It can lead to a more distant future, and I will keep walking it. So I am very, very grateful.

items.question: How have repeated paper rejections affected your response to rejection?
items.object: Repeated rejection of his research papers
items.answer: After DiT, we did another work that extended flow matching—a new objective—in the Transformer setting. It is always told as a joke too: we submitted it first, and it was rejected again, for the same reason. But again, after this happened enough times, I became basically immune. In fact, it is rather antifragile. Taleb has a book called Antifragile.

items.question: What do you mean when you say research must be an antifragile system?
items.object: Research as an antifragile system
items.answer: In my Infinite Games talk, I also mentioned this view: research must be an antifragile system. What does antifragile mean? If an organization, person, or endeavor is antifragile, then when a possible random event—a black-swan event or some shock, something surprising—occurs, its gains are greater than its losses. Then it is antifragile. But if the shock knocks it down immediately, it is fragile. So, to me, research is about making people increasingly antifragile. Then paper rejection does not make you so sad.

items.question: How do you understand the role of vision in the Cambrian explosion?
items.object: The Cambrian explosion and the evolution of vision
items.answer: I’ve explained the Cambrian this way: the leading theory says the evolution of vision brought an arms race in visual ability among species, leading to an explosion of species. So people sometimes think of the Cambrian as the beginning of vision.

items.question: How do you put the emergence of language and abstract thinking into perspective within evolutionary history?
items.object: The emergence of language and abstract thinking in evolutionary history
items.answer: From 538 million years ago until now, so-called behavioral modernity occurred only 30,000 to 50,000 years ago. If we compress everything from the Cambrian explosion, when species began appearing on Earth, to the present into one day—suppose all this happened within 24 hours—then the part involving language, behavioral modernity, abstract thinking, and symbolic reasoning occupies only the final—guess how long? Just guess.

items.question: How do you understand the place of language in human intelligence when you take a longer historical perspective?

items.answer: In the long river of history, the time we have had language is extremely, extremely short. But because we are human, we always think about and view history from the human perspective, so we feel language is naturally part of human intelligence and one of the main differences between human intelligence and other animals' intelligence.

items.question: How did you approach the Cambrian-1 project amid the excitement around multimodal large models?
items.object: The research approach behind Cambrian-1
items.answer: Amid all the excitement around multimodal large models, we wanted—somewhat like our perspective during ConvNeXt—to examine what is happening now in a solid, scientific way: what matters and what does not. That was the starting point for the Cambrian model. Before it, there was another paper called Eyes Wide Shut. That paper argued that for vision encoders, CLIP may not be optimal; it may have its own shortcomings, because too many language shortcuts can produce biases in visual understanding. Cambrian-1 is, in a sense, a continuation of that paper: how to train a system of our own, studying every component sufficiently. But there is one component we do not touch: the LM part. We do not touch it or care about it. Instead, we study the composition of our data, visual representations, and subsequent things such as all kinds of architectures for visual processing. It is quite a large effort.

items.question: How do you assess Google’s TPU Research Cloud as a resource for academic research?
items.object: Google’s TPU Research Cloud and its usefulness for academic research
items.answer: There is a foundation behind this, which is interesting to share. I just mentioned how Kaiming built infrastructure on TPUs from scratch, gained our own resources, and it led to work such as MoCo, MAE, and DiT. So later, at NYU, I naturally considered whether we could also do things on TPUs, because Google—thanks to Google—is a very generous company. It has a program called TRC, TPU Research Cloud, which gives academic students and faculty computing resources free of charge. But those resources are extremely hard to use, because the same problem remains: there is no ecosystem, no infrastructure, no codebase. Many things in PyTorch do not work on it.

items.question: How did you decide whether your students should persist with Google's difficult-to-use TPU resources?
items.object: Persisting with TPU infrastructure development in an academic research group
items.answer: This was actually the choice we faced at the beginning. On one hand, we got some resources from Google, so we could have more compute—absolute compute—to do what we wanted to do. On the other hand, this thing was just too hard to use. So I told the students, you absolutely have to give it a try. I also told them, for example, Kai-Ming’s story. But they tried it for maybe about a week, then came back and said, “Professor, we really can’t stand this. Can we buy one or two H100 machines and just use GPUs?” And I told them, we still have to be patient. If, say, you try for three to four weeks and find there really are technical obstacles—because we’re not at Google and don’t have that infrastructure, there are things we genuinely cannot do or solve—then we can give up and move on to the next thing. But if it is only temporary resistance, and you have only tried for one week and then found, hey, this is difficult, then I think we must try to step outside our comfort zone and solve some of these infrastructure problems, even if they may initially have nothing to do with research. Anyway, I persuaded the students back, and they continued developing our own infrastructure on TPUs. Why not use GPUs? No money. Universities are in a terrible state.

items.question: Why do you see running an academic research group in North America as resembling starting a company?
items.object: Funding constraints in North American academic research
items.answer:
Academia in North America is in a very, very difficult position. Mainly, first, there are not enough resources. For a simple example, say we apply for funding. The U.S. funding system—this may be drifting a little far afield—but over the past several decades it has not really grown, despite very high inflation. Everything has become expensive, and students’ tuition has become expensive too, but government support, as well as companies’ proposal-type programs and funding programs, has remained at a very low level. On average, an American government agency such as NSF can give an individual PI total funding at roughly the $500,000 level. Dollars. Over five years. So about $100,000 per year. And corporate funding has become much scarcer too, again because ChatGPT and the era of LLMs arrived, and everyone gradually started contracting. Opportunities for industry funding are also becoming fewer and fewer. And if there is a funding opportunity, it will generally give you perhaps $100,000 to $150,000, just that amount, as a one-time grant. But you know, perhaps a hundred schools, with a hundred professors or more, are competing for that $100,000. What can $100,000 do? It can support one student for a year. For tuition. What else can it do? It can buy half of an H100 or H100 cluster. Or it can buy three to four cards. So you cannot really get anything done this way.

And of course, it is not just me complaining. All of the so-called junior faculty in the U.S. are living through tremendous hardship. Everyone has to find different resources in their own way. That is also why it is a bit like starting a company: under very constrained resources, you have to find different resources in different places; you have to raise money. I say mine is not business at all, but in some places there may indeed be some commonality.

At the time I had a collaborator at Google, and he was unusual too—he never went into the office. He said, “Hey, we can talk.” I said, “Sure, I’ll come talk.” So I flew to the Bay Area to see him. He said, “We can talk, but let’s not talk in the office. Let’s go hiking on the trail beside Google.” So in the height of summer, I hiked with him for an hour, explaining some of our infrastructure contributions on TPUs, and why building a longer-term collaborative partnership would be good for Google and for us. I thought, isn’t this a fundraising process? It is begging for alms. Yes, begging for alms, exactly. And it really is, because this kind of support asks for no return. So I am very grateful to Google. But anyway, I think the people I should thank even more are these students of mine. Bit by bit, they broke through layer upon layer of difficulty. Peter, Boyang, Shusheng, and many others all made major contributions on TPUs.

items.question: How have Bi Gan's and Jia Zhangke's ideas about cinema shaped your understanding of video as a research problem?
items.object: Long takes in cinema as an inspiration for video understanding research
items.answer:
What really made me want to do this goes back to film, and is closely related to two Chinese directors I like: Director Jia, Jia Zhangke, and Bi Gan, both very famous Chinese directors. In Bi Gan’s Kaili Blues, he makes extensive use of long takes. This made me feel that, okay, although for him it is a visual tool, for humans it is also a very important medium for visual understanding. What is a long take? Living in this world is a long take; our eyes are our cameras. We keep doing all kinds of things in the world without stopping. What we see is video, but we can also see everything behind the pixels of that video. We can reason about causality and perceive space.

Jia Zhangke once said something I strongly agree with. He told me this in New York: film is interesting because if you only look at the timeline, it is a timeline, a linear timeline. But at every point on that timeline, you need a space to expand its time. Like us talking now: even though it is a static, motionless image, suppose there were a long take; or suppose you were on the streets of New York today, beneath Downing Street Bridge—you would still be seeing one frame after another. But what it actually embodies behind those frames is the state of the world, the global information of the whole space. This completely transcends what the shot encodes in each separate, individual frame. I think that makes a great deal of sense. So that made me feel that we still have to do video, even if video is hard, even if it requires processing massive amounts of data.

items.question: What direction do you want to establish for multimodal research through your Compare-S paper?
items.object: Compare-S and a progression from multimodal models toward predictive world models
items.answer:
It is somewhat like a position paper—a paper putting forward a viewpoint. We want to propose the concept of “supersensing,” of super-perception. It is also a paper about data, about structure and architecture, and about spatial intelligence. Professor Fei-Fei also gave us a great deal of valuable advice. But the core is that we want to define a paradigm: where should multimodality go next?

If you look at it step by step, perhaps using an imperfect analogy with autonomous driving: you may have an L0 system, a system with nothing—this is a large model. It cannot observe all the visual knowledge of the world. It cannot see images or video, but it can understand the world indirectly through language, like Plato’s allegory of the cave. That is fine; we call it L0. L1 is today’s multimodal system. It has somewhat better ability: it can, so to speak, show and tell. You show it something and it can tell you answers about what you showed it. You ask it a question and it gives an answer. That may be L1. Then L2, which I call streaming event cognition: it is no longer just looking at one still image. You have a continuous, streamable visual stream. Your intelligent system needs to understand and process this visual stream, answer questions, and understand what has happened. The next stage I call spatial cognition: at every point in a temporal sequence, how can you see the space behind the current frame, behind those pixels? This too is an extremely unique human ability.

Finally, I think the end state is that we need a predictive world model. Only a kind of predictive world model can tell you everything about the real world you observe. What I want to say through this paper is that we are building a ladder, step by step, toward the future of a world model. We may not know how to define a world model—at least this paper does not try to define one—but we can know which capabilities we must have. That is the core of the paper.

We also filmed a short video and I posted it on Twitter. Some students simply took a camera and filmed on the streets of New York. We spent no money, and it was not for promotion. Unfortunately, we did not manage to make a Bi Gan-style long take, but we filmed while walking; it was like a love letter to New York. Many people did not understand: “Why did you film this? Does it relate to your paper?” Of course it does. The paper itself is about an agent living in the real world: how it takes in continuous visual-stream signals and senses what is happening in the world. It may be moved by things; it may be surprised. But more often, its brain has a spontaneously operating world model guiding it—guiding it in living in the world.

I think this paper is quite interesting, because I had not previously done this kind of work that tries to set an agenda, to define a problem. So I hope to learn more from Professor Fei-Fei. Professor Fei-Fei often talks about the North Star. The question I have kept asking is: what exactly is the North Star of vision? What exactly is this problem? How should it be solved? So that is this paper.

I think this paper is quite interesting, because I had not previously done this kind of work that tries to set an agenda, to define a problem. So I hope to learn more from Professor Fei-Fei. Professor Fei-Fei often talks about the North Star. The question I have kept asking is: what exactly is the North Star of vision? What exactly is this problem? How should it be solved? So that is this paper.

items.question: How do you understand computer vision as a perspective on intelligence?
items.object: Computer vision as a perspective on intelligence
items.answer:
The term “computer vision” itself is interesting. It is called vision, and “vision” has two meanings; it is a very ambiguous word. Vision refers both to sight and to your anticipation of the future. You say someone has a lot of vision. They have a vision. Visionary—having vision. So I can say that I am someone who does computer vision. But under my definition, computer vision is a perspective. It is not a specific task, and it is not even a specific field; it is a perspective, a viewpoint. Or rather, I think it is quite fundamental to intelligence: the sum of a series of problems that intelligence must solve. Their sum. This thing is called vision.

More specifically, what is vision, or what problems does vision care about? I may not be able to explain it clearly; let me think. First, it cares about signals that are continuous in space, high-dimensional, and noisy. That is the problem computer vision must solve. Computer vision is not trying to solve the problem of writing vast amounts of text on paper and evolving some form of intelligence from that. It addresses a market—its target market is completely different from language. Continuous, high-dimensional, noisy signals: those are what vision must solve.

Second, from the first day I worked on vision—from the first paper I mentioned, DSN or this HIDE/HEE—I knew, or made this bet: the most important thing in vision is to learn hierarchical representations. This is extremely important. If your representations have no hierarchy, you have no way to solve many problems in the world. Hierarchy is a process of abstraction; abstraction is a process of generalization. This is very different from language models, because language models think about the problem purely in semantic space.

There are other characteristics too. Vision as a perspective is also massively parallel. We can see many things at once; many areas of our cerebral cortex are firing. We process many different objects in parallel, along with their causal regularities, their intuitive physics, and their physical changes. These things occur simultaneously across different times and spaces, and we have a way to capture all these changes. I think that is also an important characteristic of vision.

Finally, perhaps there is some kind of feature sharing, though I do not know how to define it. This involves semantics, or genuine understanding. If I see a dog drawn by a child, a cartoon dog, and a real dog running around in the world, how do I connect all these differently viewed entities and construct the abstract cognition that they are all dogs? They differ enormously; from the perspective of data, they are far too different, and no individual pixels are comparable. So vision has to solve—there may be more, and I have not thought this through carefully—but it has these commonalities: hierarchical structure, continuous-domain modeling, and massive parallelism and massive sharing. These are parts of intelligence. They cannot simply be reduced to a small set of problems for a computer-vision system.

items.question: How do you see the significance of computer vision as fewer students and faculty pursue it?
items.object: Computer vision as a perspective on intelligence
items.answer: I feel that computer vision—although fewer and fewer people are working in the direction now, fewer students are applying, undergraduates are less willing to choose something called computer vision, and faculties may increasingly recruit fewer professors doing pure computer vision—if you regard computer vision as a perspective, then it is an essence of intelligence.

items.question: How do you view computer vision’s apparent marginalization as large language models have risen?
items.object: Computer vision’s apparent marginalization by large language models
items.answer: I do not feel discouraged at all. As I said, I should thank LLMs. Without LLMs, vision could not have expanded into today’s genuinely broad scope of multimodal intelligence. Looking back at the history of vision, there are actually two axes you can draw. In the early stages, computer vision always handled the most singular, specific, simple tasks: MNIST digit recognition—one, two, three, four; displaying which digit it is. Then small datasets such as CIFAR: ten-way classification on 32×32 pixels—cat, dog, car, or airplane. Then ImageNet appeared: classification at roughly the 256×256 level. At that time the parameters were still relatively controllable. Later came detection and segmentation, more structured cognitive processes. That is computer vision. Then the axis continues forward to the rise of multimodal large language models. Because of the introduction of multimodality, we can readily abandon much of the fixed design of specific tasks. I can now take an image and ask all kinds of questions. Supposedly, language as a good interface can help solve many problems. So this axis moves from simple to complex tasks, but it is also an axis along which language gradually enters computer vision. There are two issues here. First, language’s entry into vision brings enormous benefits: we can define problems freely, ask anything, and get any answer. But the second major risk is that the introduction of language also makes you more and more dependent on language. So in many multimodal cases, the tasks actually have little to do with vision; they are purely language problems. From this angle, vision does seem to have become marginalized. But I would not feel discouraged. I would see it as a tremendous opportunity. When the problems you solve are relatively simple, it does not matter: if language can solve them, use language. Although I cannot do grounding—I cannot know what the “red” in the red apple you describe actually is, or what an apple actually is—somehow I can still complete certain decision tasks through statistical information in language. There is nothing wrong with that. But hidden inside is a huge opportunity: when one day we really need to deal with real tasks in the real world and build some kind of real intelligence, then today’s imperfect visual representations will become a major deficiency. So Yann LeCun’s view is that everyone is currently just leaning on a crutch, and that crutch is the language model itself. You can walk, and you may feel, hey, I walk pretty well, but perhaps you cannot run or compete in the Olympics. Because one of your legs—the leg of visual representation—is still not good enough.

items.question: What do you mean when you distinguish LLMs from intelligence that interacts with the real world?
items.object: LLMs and the distinction between digital intelligence and intelligence that interacts with the real world
items.answer: Because I think an LLM is—well, an LLM is virtual intelligence. Perhaps “virtual” is the wrong word. By real, I mean interacting with the real world. The point is that the problems LLMs currently solve very well mostly still occur in digital space.

items.question: How do you distinguish the problems LLMs solve well from the problems vision needs to solve?
items.object: The distinction between LLM applications and problems addressed by vision
items.answer: For example, an LLM can memorize all this factual knowledge. We can store all of Wikipedia’s articles inside it, and it can tell us everything we want to know. It can be a very good legal adviser; it can even help summarize knowledge and provide education. LLMs are of course revolutionary. But to me, this is a completely different market from the problems that vision as a perspective must solve, where what you need to handle is a continuous, high-dimensional, noisy domain.

items.question: How do you see the role of visual intelligence in moving from language models to genuinely general-purpose robotics?
items.object: Visual intelligence as a bridge between language models and general-purpose robotics
items.answer:
To me there are two extremes. But these spaces are not only about robots, by the way. Robotics is one very good example. These things are hard to tokenize. They have already departed from virtual space and digital space. There are also many industrial applications, such as industrial-process control. All tasks involving sensor-environment signals: you have many different sensors that sense what is happening in the world, and you need a unified algorithm to model this environment, this system, so that when you perform an action or intervention, you can predict what changes will happen next in the system. That is difficult for an LM to do.

At one extreme, LMs are very good at doing many things in digitized space, and at using coding as an interface—through agents—to intervene in our physical lives. That will happen too, and there is no problem with it. But ultimately it is still based on discrete tokens, on a token position. At the far right is robotics, but not simple robotics: it must be genuinely general-purpose robotics, able to generalize to the degree that it can do everything humans can do. It has its own role system and its own brain.

What I feel now is that, between these two poles, how to derive robotics step by step from LMs—that is the problem computer vision, or visual intelligence in the new era, needs to solve. And I think that is also the future of multimodality. Clearly, robotics does not work yet. I often tell students and people around me that what I most want to do is solve the robotics problem by not doing robotics.

items.question: Why do you want to focus on the robot brain rather than get involved in robot hardware early?
items.object: Focusing on the robot brain rather than building robot hardware
items.answer: It is because I think robotics is progressing too quickly. The things being discussed in chats now and so on are all rather staggering. But on the other hand, someone still has to focus on pretraining—on what this so-called robot brain actually is. Or that brain includes your visual system. As for control and hardware, it is a case of brothers climbing a mountain, each making their own effort. I do not need to get involved in hardware too early. There are fundamental research problems at the software layer that have not been solved, problems in constructing the brain that have not been solved; we need to concentrate on solving that part first. Of course, many people would argue that you must have a closed loop, some form of collaboration, and validate on robots; otherwise an algorithm or model you build may not be usable. I completely agree with that too, but I think it can happen through partnerships. I simply do not want to—also, I have no money; I cannot buy so many robots. Robots have their own hardware scaling law, by the way: you need to buy many robots to do hardware well. I want to focus on the brain. I think that is a problem computer vision must solve, representation learning must solve, and ultimately world models must solve.

items.question: How do you think about the need for scaling laws in computer vision?
items.object: Scaling laws in computer vision
items.answer: First, one cannot say they came so much earlier, because CV does not yet have a scaling law, right? Before, all of us were very desperate: why does vision never have such a scaling law? It may be better now. For example, video diffusion has some scaling behavior: so-called scaling means you can consume more data and get better results. Or, in a more abstract characterization, a scaling law says that if you have a transformer system and satisfy a ratio like C equals 6ND—your compute is basically six times the product of tokens and the number of parameters. I want to use this abstract definition to say that I increasingly feel vision does not need a scaling law.

items.question: Why do you regard language modeling as strongly supervised learning?
items.object: Language modeling as strongly supervised learning
items.answer: My view—not necessarily a provocative claim, but a long-term view, and many NLP people agree—is that language modeling is not really self-supervised learning; it is strongly supervised learning. That depends on how you define supervision. Usually, whether you have external annotation or labels determines whether learning is self-supervised or strongly supervised. But language is an exceptional case. What is language? Over thousands of years of civilization, humans have continually evolved it and processed everything about the world, both sociologically and as individual people, then stored it in tokenized form. By chance, we have the Internet, and we uploaded all that knowledge to it. For every LM researcher, that is free. But something being free does not mean it has no labels. Suppose there were no Internet: could you still train a language model?

items.question: How do you see the strengths and limitations of language models as a foundation for a model of the world?
items.object: Language models as the foundation of a world model
items.answer: I think this uploading of knowledge is itself a process of constructing supervision. So it differs from vision. It is as though language tries to solve problems while always remaining in the target Y-space. Normally, we talk about a mapping from X to Y in machine learning. Regardless of where X and Y are, that is how you can define the problem. Usually Y is the supervision, the label, and X is your data. You can regard the language model as describing only things in Y-space. But that is not enough to represent the entirety of the world. Many things cannot be described or characterized through language. This is both language’s advantage and, as I said, possibly why it may eventually wither away, or why LMs will not be the foundation of the entire world model. Its advantage is that you need do nothing to align with people.

items.question: How do you understand the limitations of language as a tool for representing what an intelligent system should model?
items.object: Language as a communication tool and its limitations for intelligent systems
items.answer: Language is a communication tool. It is not a thinking tool, and not even a decision-making tool; it is communication, an instrument of exchange. So if it is a communication tool, you always have to make trade-offs; you always have to sacrifice something. It aligns very well with people as a communication tool, but at the same time it loses many things that an intelligent system should model. For example, we say, “I have a cup; it fell to the ground and shattered.” That is language. We say it because it is what is best suited to communication; we care only about the outcome and state. We do not care exactly how a cup shattered when it fell, which physical laws it obeyed, what dynamics lay behind it, what its dynamics were. We do not care about those things. So I think that is also its limitation.

items.question: How do you view the concern that adding vision could make an AI system less intelligent?
items.object: Vision in multimodal AI systems
items.answer: Yes, I agree: one should not use a stupid multimodal system. But I think that if you do not add vision, you will definitely be very stupid. The root issue is how you define smart and stupid.

items.question: How do you understand Moravec’s paradox in terms of what makes a task easy or difficult for AI?
items.object: Moravec’s paradox
items.answer: Over the past several decades, we AI researchers have continually run into Moravec’s paradox. It says that, for machines, the easy things are hard and the hard things are easy: things that are easy for machines are hard for humans; things that are hard for machines are easy for humans.
quotes: Over the past several decades, AI researchers have continually run into Moravec’s paradox. It says that, for machines, the easy things are hard and the hard things are easy: things that are easy for machines are hard for humans; things that are hard for machines are easy for humans.

items.question: How do you think people arrive at an answer to a question about something in their visual surroundings?
items.object: How people answer questions about their visual surroundings
items.answer: When we look at the world around us, say I ask you a question: what color is the trash can beside you? You would not directly give me an answer like a language model. You would first think: where is the trash can? You might turn your head, discover a refrigerator there, and perhaps the trash can is beside it.

items.question: How do you look back on your experience with the V-Star paper?

items.answer: I think this is worth discussing because for me it was a bittersweet lesson. The bitter part is—let me first tell you what happened. After we had this paper, we had our own benchmark. I have two friends, Alex Kirilov, who is also an author of SAM, and Bowen; both work at OpenAI.

items.question: What did seeing your university research inspire OpenAI researchers mean to you?
items.object: University research’s ability to inspire OpenAI researchers
items.answer: What comforted me is that it was the first time I felt we could really take a different path, and that this could somehow inspire OpenAI researchers to improve their own model. At least, it made me feel there are things we can do in universities.

items.question: Why did you value the acknowledgment of DiT in OpenAI’s Sora blog post?
items.object: The acknowledgment of DiT in OpenAI’s Sora blog post
items.answer: For me, the bitter part is that back then, at OpenAI—when Sora came out, people could accept DiT because DiT was cited in Sora’s blog post, or its name was there, so people could trace the logic and its sources.

items.question: How do you view the changing openness of industry research labs over the past few years?
items.object: The increasing closedness of industry research labs
items.answer: Unfortunately, over the past few years, industry research labs have become increasingly closed. At first everyone published papers; later they could no longer publish papers but could write blog posts.
quotes: But unfortunately, over the past few years, industry research labs have become increasingly closed. At first everyone published papers; later they could no longer publish papers but could write blog posts.
