items.question: How do you view industry research blog posts replacing individual researchers’ names with bylines like “OpenAI team” or “Gemini team”?
items.object: Individual credit in industry research publications
items.answer: They could include citations and list every team member’s name. Later, they could publish a blog post but could no longer have bylines—only “OpenAI team” or “Gemini team,” and that was it. So I think this may interrupt what could have been a very healthy channel of exchange between academia and industry. Research, in essence, is still something we do for love. We explore these questions not because it will necessarily deliver a product or make money. But some form of credit assignment—letting people know who did what—has been a mechanism that supported academia’s progress over the past decades.

items.question: How do you understand the contribution of REPA (Representation Alignment)?
items.object: REPA (Representation Alignment)
items.answer: It opened up, at least, a small research domain. What it does is simple. Essentially it is a deeply supervised net: a model has not only a diffusion loss at the top, its final objective, but also additional objectives drawn out in the middle. The objective we use is to make a diffusion model—a generative model, by the way—align its internal representation with the representation of an external self-supervised model.

items.question: Why do you think generative models should use strong representations more directly?
items.object: Representation as a foundation for generative models
items.answer: Again, the point this year is that representation is the most important thing. It is important not only for multimodal understanding in systems such as Comprehend-1, but also for generative models that generate images and videos. This was a major inspiration for me, but it has not gone far enough. Why use deep supervision, such an indirect way, to do alignment? What if we could directly use a strong representation as an encoder for the generative model, or as its foundation?

items.question: How do you view the concern that generating images in a high-dimensional representation makes learning harder?
items.object: High-dimensional representations in machine learning
items.answer: Our results were completely the opposite. The paper is called RE, Representation Autoencoder. When I visited Hong Kong, a student asked whether the dimension of our autoencoder’s representation layer was too high, whether it might make the learning system more complicated or training harder. It is a representation, not a simple original pixel representation and not a low-dimensional VAE representation. Professor Ma Yi became very excited, stood up, and said, “I want to tell everyone, earnestly: you must not be afraid of high dimensionality.” I think he said something very right. High dimensionality is a very, very important cornerstone of all machine learning. Whether it is older kernel methods, or why transformers need an up-projection layer—taking a low-dimensional vector and making it four times larger and wider through a fully connected layer—all of it tells the same fact: in a high-dimensional space, many problems that cannot be solved in low-dimensional space can now be solved. Information absent from low-dimensional space can exist there, and you can have better efficiency. This is the same logic as traditional machine-learning theory: lift dimensions so your data points can become linearly separable. I was greatly encouraged by the phrasing: do not fear high dimensionality.

items.question: Why do you see RE, the Representation Autoencoder, as an important step in your research?
items.object: RE (Representation Autoencoder) as a departure from the VAE framework
items.answer: Because people are often afraid—not only of high-dimensional representations, but of escaping a current local optimum. Much of what we did before was aimed at jumping out of this local optimum. VAE is one local optimum of the current era. We hoped to connect everything through representation learning, and that is natural in one sense. Many people now have related papers, and many concurrent works are excellent. But in another sense it is not so natural, because you need to jump out of the original framework to do something new. When you can jump out of that local optimum and do something new, you feel your world open up. RE is an important work for us, or for my research, because it tells me something, or lets me make a bet and predict a future. Whether it is right or wrong, we can look again in a few years. It is also related to language and to diffusion models such as the recently popular CDance and Sora.

items.question: How do you think representation learning will change the role of large language models in future AI systems?
items.object: Representation learning as the foundation of future AI
items.answer: My bet is that there is only one important thing in the world: how to learn representation. Once you have a sufficiently good representation, handling other problems on top of it is easy. Your language model will gradually degrade into a simple communication interface. It will not be like now, where all multimodal intelligence is driven by a large language model and the representation layer merely provides a little bit of context. Most of the so-called heavy lifting, all the dirty and tiring work, is done by the large language model. The bet I want to make is that the future will not be like this. In the future, you will have a very good foundation. It is a very good representation, but it is also a very good world model. We can discuss what a world model means later, but this foundation may not be a checkpoint. It may be a cognitive architecture of multiple components—neural modules connected together. That sounds complicated, but essentially it is your brain. It has different regions handling different things. Language—the LLM layer—will gradually degrade into an interface to this foundational representation, or world model. It is still very important and will never disappear, because people need a large language model to pose questions and answer questions.

items.question: How do you understand what a world model is?
items.object: World models
items.answer: Strictly speaking, I understand a world model as taking the state of a system or an environment—say its state at the current time. It is not necessarily only doing temporal prediction. But setting that aside: you have a system or environment with a state St, right? Then you have an intervention or action, say At. You apply an action to the system at the current time, and you want to learn a predictive function, or transition function, f, that can take your action and your current state, the state of the environment.

items.question: Why do you see the basic concept of a world model as straightforward rather than new?
items.object: World models as a longstanding concept for guiding actions
items.answer: I think the definition itself is extremely direct, even a bit trivial, because this is not a new concept. In 1943, there was a physiologist, I think, named Kenneth Craik. He first proposed this concept. He said that people have such a world model in their minds. It can tell us what consequences will occur when we take a given action. Because we can predict the consequences brought by our actions, that can guide what actions we should take and what decisions to make. If I know that putting my hand into a fire will hurt, I will not put my hand into the fire. This predictive structure has also been used in control theory, including in the 1960s and ’70s, when people were figuring out how to send a lunar probe to the Moon or somewhere else. They needed such control systems. A classic algorithm, model predictive control, also involves a model, which is in fact a kind of world model. The algorithm is very simple: determine which control signal to apply to the system so that it completes a specified task.

items.question: How do you understand the role of future prediction in model predictive control?
items.object: Model predictive control
items.answer: What I do at the current time is roll out through my model an action sequence. That is, I output the action sequence I will take next, use the model and that sequence to obtain the next state, or the state at every step, and finally have some kind of cost function, a metric. It tells me how far I am from my ultimate goal after executing that action sequence. So the algorithm is very simple: continually sample action sequences, go back to step one, find the action sequence with the lowest cost, execute its first step, and repeat this iteratively—then roll out the next action sequence. Thus, every decision is based on a prediction of the future.

items.question: What do you find interesting about Rich Sutton’s framing of human intelligence in his Dyna paper?
items.object: Rich Sutton’s Dyna paper and its framing of human intelligence
items.answer: I find the view, or frame, very interesting: human intelligence may have two kinds of systems—one a reactive policy, and one a more intelligent model-based policy. The analogy is System 1 and System 2. Human cognition has “thinking fast” and “thinking slow.” For difficult problems, we may need more mental cycles to study them.

items.question: How do you understand the change in decision-making as you become an experienced driver?
items.object: Learning to drive and internalizing decisions
items.answer: When we first learn to drive, we are extremely nervous, looking left and right and making many decisions. Once we truly know how to drive, we internalize those decisions as part of our muscle memory.

items.question: What do you find interesting about Rich Sutton’s argument for world models in the Dyna paper?
items.object: Rich Sutton’s Dyna paper and its argument for world models
items.answer: Rich Sutton says something interesting in the Dyna paper. He asks, “What is reinforcement learning?” Reinforcement learning is a very primitive, basic, model-free learning algorithm without this world model. So Rich Sutton himself was somewhat against pure reinforcement learning, at least at that time in that paper. He says a better system is of course one with a sufficiently strong world model, one that can predict the next state from the current state. Then it has the capability for planning—meaning the ability to make plans.

items.question: How do you understand the essence of a world model?

items.answer: I see planning and reasoning as, in a sense, the same concept. Reasoning is very popular in large language models now, but planning, and planning’s significance for decision-making, were already being discussed long ago in control theory and reinforcement learning. So this is a history of world models. From this perspective, the essence of a world model is how to characterize a system and environment such that you can make predictions within it, and those predictions can guide your action sequences and your own decisions.

items.answer: Why do I call it a characterization unit with minimal information? Suppose we are talking about the physical world—the Earth, say, or let’s not go that far; let’s take this room. This too is an environment. What characterizes the state of this environment? If you do not seek minimal information, or minimum description length, it could mean reconstructing the whole space and meticulously characterizing all parameters in the system: the texture of the table, sound waves, the mass of the table, and all kinds of physical parameters of this microphone.

items.question: How do you think a state should represent an environment for decision-making?
items.object: Task-dependent states and hierarchical representation learning
items.answer: I only need to know some basic facts. For example, that my microphone can sit on the table. I do not care about the lighting at every point, nor every tiny detail of the table’s texture. None of that matters. So a state can contain a great deal of information, or enough information. That depends on the task you are solving. How do you construct such a state? This is directly connected to representation learning. Representation learning, as I just said, requires hierarchical representation. The purpose is to gradually develop representations layer by layer, iteratively, that become increasingly abstract and increasingly meaningful and valuable for decision-making.

items.question: How do you illustrate the level of detail involved in modeling an airplane’s dynamics from the lowest level?
items.object: Modeling an airplane’s dynamics at the molecular level
items.answer: Say we want to build an airplane and model its dynamical system to know how it can use less effort and fuel. We could start at the lowest level and say that every square or cubic centimeter may contain ten-to-the-ten-something molecules, model every molecular collision, and characterize the system that way.

items.question: How do you see latent representations outside language in relation to the bitter lesson?
items.object: Latent representations outside language and the bitter lesson
items.answer: People can infer indirectly what representation you have learned, or which representations are meaningful; that is not a problem. It is not a complete black box. But it is not constrained by the syntax and logic of language. This is why I say LLMs are completely insufficiently bitter-lesson. The bitter lesson says you should reduce human knowledge as much as possible.

items.question: How do you view language as a way of characterizing the world?
items.object: Language as a way of characterizing the world
items.answer: I think we should reduce human arrogance, its so-called conceit, its cleverness, and such clever structures as much as possible; and use search and learning as much as possible to find answers. But if we are discussing how to characterize the world, language is precisely such a structure. Language is an extremely clever human product. It has exquisite design.

items.question: Why do you agree that language models are not controllable or safe?
items.object: Language models' controllability, safety, and alignment
items.answer: I quite agree that LMs are not controllable or safe. They do not have a real world model. Even if we use an LM as a world model, it is fundamentally flawed—a defective world model. All current controllability or safety is designed and achieved through fine-tuning: feed it lots of data so it knows what to do and not do, what it cannot do, what it may or may not say, what might cause danger, and what is friendlier. This is called alignment. But all of it comes from post-training or fine-tuning alignment.

items.question: How do you think a true world model could make an AI system's behavior safer?
items.object: True world models and safe AI behavior
items.answer: The way I see it, with a true world model, you can predict what consequences your actions will lead to. You can understand the outcomes of your behavior and avoid it during inference. You can add external constraints saying, hey, you really cannot do this. For example, a robot is cutting vegetables with a knife. How do I ensure that it does not turn around and slash you?

items.question: Why do you think world models are so hard to define?
items.object: World models as a shared goal across different technical approaches
items.answer: I think the reason world models are hard to define is that they are not a technical route or an algorithm; they are a goal. Whether you are making LMs, video diffusion models, or Gaussian splatting, all of us are on the road toward world models. So I think some of this competition and these arguments will look extraordinarily ridiculous in one or two years. We are all moving along this route, and everyone knows it is the road that ought to lead in the right direction; people are just thinking about it from different directions.

items.question: Why do you think spatial intelligence in a 3D design setting requires an explicit 3D representation?

items.answer: In this setting I think you need a very concrete 3D form—you can call it a representation, and it is a kind of representation—but it is not an abstract concept hidden in your parameters. items.question: How do you frame the challenge of using an LLM approach to handle visual perception?
items.object: The high frequency of visual perception as a challenge for LLM approaches
items.answer: If we turn our heads just five or ten degrees, hundreds of frames are generated. The frequency is extremely high; humans can perceive changes at frequencies such as 100 hertz. If you handled this using an LLM approach, what would happen?

items.question: How do you understand the way current LLM-based approaches represent a sequence of visual frames?
items.object: Current LLM-based approaches to representing visual frames
items.answer: At least with the current approach, I would tokenize every frame, flatten it and string it into an extremely long sequence. I might downsample each frame or whatever, but string them together. If I have 256 tokens for one frame and now have 32 or 128 frames, I concatenate them, and then I have 256 times 128 tokens.

items.question: Why do you think language-modeling techniques cannot solve the problem of understanding continuous spatial signals?
items.object: Language-modeling techniques for understanding continuous spatial signals
items.answer: Behind a representation of this kind of world, there is some global state. You serialize it into extremely redundant tokens. And although people say transformers have no inductive bias, I think they do have some: their inductive bias is that they must pay equal attention to every single token. That itself is unreasonable. It means language-modeling techniques cannot solve cognition of continuous spatial signals.

items.object: Requirements for a world-model-based system

items.question: How do you distinguish the world model in our brains from a language model?
items.object: World models and language models
items.answer: As I said, the world model in our brains does a great deal in the background. There are even counterintuitive psychological findings suggesting that the brain has already made a decision for you. If there are three buttons on my table, before I know which button I want to press, one can already detect that my brain has made the decision. This experiment seems to be called the Libet experiment or something; it is controversial. But it shows that many things are already happening in the background of your brain; that is part of your world model. A language model is not like that. Language is only a communication tool: you always have a purpose, pose a question, and want an answer.

items.question: How do you understand the shift from modeling language or labels to modeling the data itself in video-generation models?
items.object: Video generation as modeling data rather than language or label distributions
items.answer: With video-generation models, you model something like Px given y. That means what you model now is x: x is the data itself, and y becomes a condition. To me, that is already very different. With a low-dimensional y space, your probability density only competes within the distribution of y—that is, the likelihood you assign. Let’s not talk about language models; take a thousand-class classifier. Those labels are also a precursor of language, a low-dimensional vocabulary. If you do such a classification problem, all the decisions are: if this is a cat, it cannot be a dog. It is constrained by the label set. But when you model Px given y—when you make a generative model—the likelihood you assign concerns what phenomena and things are more likely to exist in the world. That is very different. The information in the intelligence you need to learn is far greater than in modeling Py. You need to know why a four-legged cat is more common than a three-legged cat. If I generate a video—say, a running video—why is a smooth running state more credible and more likely than sudden hallucinations of three legs or four legs? More likely in probability space. The information content is enormous: what you must model far exceeds what you characterize in language space or label space. You need some cognition of the world. So to me this is a little more bitter-lesson: you abandon more cognition, logic, and syntax from language space and begin modeling pixels themselves. But one step further, pixels may also be wrong; pixels themselves may not be bitter-lesson enough.

items.question: How do you understand the role of a world model in AI systems that understand and generate content?
items.object: World models as the foundation for understanding and generation
items.answer: It depends on what you want. It can show it to people. But showing people is not the core of a world model; it is the interface of a world model. The world model itself spontaneously learns better representations and makes better predictions. That has nothing to do with whether it generates a cool video, or whether it can answer information about its input space. So again, to repeat what I wanted to say: every one of us is moving forward on the path toward world models. A world model is a goal, not a specific route—not a specific algorithm or technical route. One day we will have a better world model; language models will sit above it and become stronger; we will have better multimodal models that understand the world better; and better video-generation models. There is also the popular notion of a unified model or omni model: people try to stack all data together so one system can both understand and generate. They discuss whether understanding helps generation, or generation helps understanding. I do not think that matters. Understanding and generation are one; both need a real world model as their foundation. Once you have a good world model that can make predictions, planning, and reasoning, the upper-layer decoding is very, very simple.

items.question: How do you assess the idea that “compression is intelligence” as an explanation for language-model scaling?
items.object: “Compression is intelligence” and language-model scaling laws
items.answer: What it means is that a language model is a lossless compression process—or that when a language model gets bigger and performs better, it is not because it has memorized everything by rote, but because it is a stronger model that can compress all its input information at a better rate, giving it some generalization ability. I agree, but I want to step back: because of what language models themselves care about, there is some padding in their scaling law. They do not need to use the smallest model to answer questions by genuinely understanding the world. That is the world model itself.

items.question: What potential do you see in always-on AI wearables powered by world models?

items.answer: I think this is a microcosm of a future world model in AI wearables. If there really were glasses—or some wearable device—that could truly be always on, setting aside power-consumption and hardware issues, and see in real time everything we can see—with a completely always-on, infinite stream of tokens entering the system, I think this has enormous potential. I would really want it, because I want to know when I drank coffee and whether drinking it an hour earlier or later caused poorer sleep that night. Or if I were an athlete, it could guide every movement. items.question: How do you see world models in relation to the broader development of AI?

items.answer: I actually don’t think there’s been a leap. As I’ve just been saying all along, I think representation learning, supervised learning, world models, and the development of AI as a whole have actually been quite a smooth transition. And I’m actually not that fond of the term “world model” anymore. I think it sounds a little hyped, and now it has become this catch-all, bag-like label, and everyone claims they are doing world models. On the one hand, I think this is definitely not a process that a researcher would enjoy. But on the other hand, perhaps for a field to move forward, it still needs some buzzwords like this. If I had to name one thing I like about “world model,” it might be that—the so-called world model—one thing about it is something Jitendra Malik, a professor at Berkeley, said. He said the one thing he likes about “world model” is that it tells people I work on a world model, not a word model—word as in W-O-R-D. I work on a world model, not a word model. items.question: Why do you think world models need the real world?
items.object: World models’ dependence on the real world
items.answer: LLMs cannot solve every problem. World models also need the world. The world has two parts. The first is the ability to define problems—the definition of problems. I hope it comes from life, from people’s real needs, or from needs in industrial production. These things are also invisible to the Silicon Valley or LLM narrative. Then there is the data issue. Although at first we can get data from the internet to train these models, ultimately we still have to pan for gold in the real world. This data is invisible too; people do not upload it to YouTube. Data on YouTube has a distribution that is very, very aligned with humans—with human values or human needs for entertainment. And we are only discussing visual data, but there is vast non-visual data in the world: data in continuous domains, high-dimensional and possibly noisy signals. I think this data is again crucial for training a world model. Our world model is not just a vision model, because the world is not only vision. But this data is currently invisible; we need to obtain it from somewhere. So these are some of the high-level thoughts from my conversations with Yann.

items.question: What do you admire about Yann LeCun?
items.object: Yann LeCun
items.answer: I think Yann is someone who can truly bend the reality field. He is incredibly impressive. Whenever I start to have doubts about something, I am willing to talk with him. He easily makes people around him—at least that is how I feel—feel a certain calm, feel that these challenges are not challenges and that the road ahead is bright. He has that ability. And of course, I deeply admire his research vision too. Things like what a world model is and why you need to filter information—this is also the core of the JEPA idea he proposed: you cannot make a generative model; you cannot memorize and reconstruct everything. You need to make predictions in an abstract representation space. That is the core of JEPA. But what I want to say is that Yann really practices what he preaches. He himself is quite JEPA: he consistently sticks to his logic and what he believes is right, without being disturbed by anything external. But that does not mean he is stubborn and incapable of listening. That is not the case. Sometimes he is wrong, sometimes he is right—he is right most of the time—but he can listen to what people say.

items.question: Why do you regard AGI as a false proposition?

items.answer: There are many interesting things—for instance chimpanzees. This author, De Waal, also wrote another book, I think called Chimpanzee Politics. items.question: What do you find compelling about Rich Sutton’s claim that building squirrel intelligence is harder than achieving feats such as coding or going to Mars?

items.answer: I was recently inspired by a theory Rich Sutton gave on a podcast, because before that I did not know how to address this. People say, aren’t LMs amazing? They can write code, win IMO and IOI gold medals, help us go to the Moon and Mars. That is so great. I cannot deny it; it really is impressive. But I think Rich Sutton’s answer was excellent. He said: Do you think this is great, impressive, difficult? Then think so, because I do not. I think the difficult problem is building the intelligence of a squirrel. Once you have squirrel intelligence—once you can build one that can survive in the real world, has its own goals, its own intrinsic reward as you said, knows hunger, has emotions, and can participate in some social activity—then writing code and going to Mars or the Moon are the easiest things imaginable. But I think Rich Sutton’s answer was excellent. He said: Do you think this is great, impressive, difficult? Then think so, because I do not. I think the difficult problem is building the intelligence of a squirrel.

Once you have squirrel intelligence—once you can build one that can survive in the real world, has its own goals, its own intrinsic reward as you said, knows hunger, has emotions, and can participate in some social activity—then writing code and going to Mars or the Moon are the easiest things imaginable.

I am gradually coming to strongly agree. If we set aside human arrogance, building squirrel intelligence is actually a harder problem. But that is not how it appears to humans, to our cognition; that is entirely because of human arrogance.

He is not viewing this from a human, anthropocentric perspective; he is viewing it from the perspective of the universe and a creator. From that perspective, recreating a squirrel is far greater than the things your human civilization created in the last eight seconds of five hundred and thirty million years. In that sense, I think it is elevated—perhaps a bit grandiose, but it makes sense.

items.question: How do you think about intelligence as a guide to what world models should solve next?

items.answer: As for defining intelligence, I would not want to give it a definition. Different animals have different intelligences, and humans have human-level intelligence. What I hope to encourage people to do is not only focus on things that each of us cannot do. Look at things we already do very well, things a four-year-old or a child of a few years old can do well. Those are in fact the problems world models need to focus on solving next.

items.question: How do you understand the frustration that comes with being a researcher?
items.object: The emotional experience of research and discussion during the current AI wave
items.answer: I feel frustrated every day. I think that has become a researcher’s fate. I think everyone’s underlying emotional tone is rather bleak, because the process of seeking through research is a process of feeling one’s way through a place without light. When you cannot see the light, you always feel lost and frustrated. The times when people truly feel joy are no more than when you actually make something work, but that part is very, very brief—perhaps only five or ten percent. Kaiming seems to have said something similar. Over time, everyone’s psychological state is rather worrying. But I think it is okay. This era is not quite like the past: there is more discussion now. I think that is one benefit brought by this wave of AI—at least people do not feel they are exploring alone in a confined space. You can scroll Xiaohongshu, Weibo, Zhihu, and see how others discuss these things. Sometimes that is quite stress-relieving.

When I watch his talks, I translate and make associations every time. I discover, oh, under my current cognitive framework, what he says can be explained this way. items.question: How has everyday life in New York changed your understanding of what AI researchers should be doing?
items.object: Everyday life in New York as a source of understanding AI
items.answer: I think this must go beyond the limitations of research and researchers, and into real life—to understand what happens in the real world. New York is very different. Every day when I go to work, first of all, I do not need to drive, so I have already begun to shed a kind of armor and enter real life by walking. That has many wonderful effects. Sometimes I am still under a lot of pressure, and sometimes things make me quite frustrated. But every time I pass through the park between my home and my university office, Washington Square Park, there are all kinds of people—every kind of person—living their own lives. There are piano-playing performers, dancers, mothers pushing strollers, old men playing chess, young people sitting on the steps doing nothing and daydreaming, and NYU students studying with laptops. My most stress-relieving time each day is this five- to ten-minute walk. I realize the world is much larger than we imagine. Not everyone cares what AI is; they may not care about it and have their own lives. The world is big. Yet AI may indeed affect their lives someday in the future. So what should we do? As researchers, do we have some social responsibility? Perhaps that is getting a bit far afield, but being in contact with more people and people living in this world has given me new understandings of what AI is and how to make the next generation of AI.

items.question: What makes Gödel, Escher, Bach a meaningful book for you?
items.object: Gödel, Escher, Bach: An Eternal Golden Braid
items.answer: One book that I suppose people often recommend—but why it mattered greatly to my life, well, I should not say it changed my life greatly. It is a collective memory from my undergraduate years. We all read a book called GEB—Gödel, Escher, Bach. Its Chinese title is Gödel, Escher, Bach: An Eternal Golden Braid. It talks about philosophy, mathematical logic, and these three people: Gödel, Bach, and Escher—a mathematician, a musician and composer, and an artist. items.question: Why do you object to using quotations from Wittgenstein and Feynman to endorse AI models?
items.object: Using Wittgenstein and Feynman quotations to endorse AI models
items.answer: When I say I’m letting go of Wittgenstein, I mean: everyone, don’t keep invoking Wittgenstein so aggressively, and then use “the limits of my language mean the limits of my world,” right, as an endorsement of an LM or linguistic determinism. That is completely absurd. And likewise, there are other examples. For instance, people cite Feynman saying, “What I cannot create, I do not understand,” as an endorsement of a unified model. I find both of these things really unacceptable.

items.question: How do you understand Wittgenstein’s claim that the limits of language are the limits of your world in relation to today’s language models?
items.object: Wittgenstein’s conception of language and its relevance to language models
items.answer: When he originally said that the limits of language are the limits of my world, there was a very strong premise behind it. In the Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus, what he was saying was that the language he meant referred to the boundaries of the world that can be characterized in propositions. Right. And that does not stand for the general entirety of what we call the world. So first, the language and world he was talking about are already different from the language and world we talk about in LMs today. Second, in his later period Wittgenstein completely overturned his earlier whole philosophical system. He later stopped saying this, and what he said instead was that language is actually a game—the concept of language games. That is, language itself has no meaning; these symbols themselves have no meaning whatsoever. They come to have meaning because they enter into a relationship with real-world practice.

items.question: How do you interpret Feynman’s statement “What I cannot create, I do not understand” when people use it to endorse a unified model?
items.object: Feynman’s quotation “What I cannot create, I do not understand” as an endorsement of a unified model
items.answer: There is nothing wrong with the sentence itself, but by create and understand he meant, for example, that we have a world, right? We need to understand this world; we need to transform this world; we need to understand the world by transforming it. Whatever—what he was talking about still involved some kind of action in a real, concrete world. Even if you are teaching a class and making a PPT, it is still a process of creation. But now many people take this sentence as an endorsement of some simple unified system. That does not hold up logically either. We cannot simply reduce creation to the loss of a diffusion model doing backpropagation. That is completely absurd. I don’t know. I think maybe it’s because I used too many famous quotations when writing essays as a child; now I get a bit of PTSD when I see these things. And I think, as Kaiming said, people can read more philosophy. I think that is quite interesting.
